notes.meaning: God told Moses to instruct the new generation of Israel to bring their regular offerings at the appointed times. Calling these sacrifices His food and a pleasing aroma was picture language showing that the Lord accepted and took delight in their worship. It reminds believers that true worship belongs to God and should always be offered on His terms.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars propose that the calendar of offerings in Numbers 28–29 was compiled in its final form by later editors from earlier Mosaic regulations, while still reflecting authentic Mosaic tradition.

notes.meaning: God commanded Israel to offer two healthy year-old male lambs each day as a regular burnt offering. In a burnt offering, the whole animal was consumed on the altar by fire, picturing total surrender to the Lord. Offering an unblemished lamb morning and evening formed the daily foundation of Israel's worship.

One lamb was sacrificed in the morning and the other at twilight, framing the entire day in worship. Each lamb was presented with a grain offering of fine flour mixed with pure olive oil. These offerings expressed daily gratitude to God for life, food, and His ongoing care.

This daily sacrifice had first been commanded at Mount Sinai when God made His covenant with Israel. Because the older generation had passed away during thirty-eight years of wandering, God reaffirmed the law for their children as they prepared to enter the Promised Land. It shows that God's people must hold fast to His unchanging commands through every generation.

Along with each lamb, the priest poured out about a quart of wine or fermented drink at the altar in the sanctuary area. This drink offering was poured out entirely to God, showing that the best of the harvest belonged to Him. It encourages God's people to offer their best without holding anything back.

The second lamb was offered at twilight with the exact same grain and drink offerings as the morning sacrifice. God required the same wholehearted devotion at the close of the day as at the start. Walking with God means seeking Him continually from morning until night.

Every weekly Sabbath day, the priests offered two extra lambs with double the grain and drink offerings. These were added on top of the regular daily morning and evening sacrifices, never replacing them. The additional gifts honored the Sabbath as a special day set apart for resting and worshipping the Lord.

At the start of each month, marked by the new moon, Israel presented a large burnt offering of two bulls, one ram, and seven lambs. This national festival marked the passage of time with public thanksgiving for God's renewal of earthly blessings. It also guarded Israel from worshiping the moon like the surrounding nations did.

Each animal in the monthly sacrifice was paired with a specific amount of fine flour mixed with oil. The bulls received the largest grain offering, the ram received less, and each lamb received a tenth of an ephah. God desires orderly, thoughtful worship where gifts are given in right proportion.

Drink offerings of wine were poured out alongside each animal, scaled from half a hin for a bull down to a quarter hin for a lamb. These monthly offerings were to be faithfully repeated at every new moon throughout the entire year. Giving God the first of each month helped keep the nation's calendar centered on Him.

Along with the burnt offerings, one male goat was sacrificed as a sin offering. While burnt offerings showed total dedication, sin offerings asked for God's pardon and cleansed the people from guilt. Even on days of joyful celebration, worshipers were reminded of their need for God's forgiving mercy.

Passover took place on the fourteenth day of the first month, followed on the fifteenth day by the week-long Feast of Unleavened Bread. Passover remembered how God spared the firstborn sons of Israel in Egypt, while the flat bread recalled how quickly they had to leave. Remembering God's great rescues gives His people confidence in His daily care.

The first day of the feast was a holy assembly where all regular daily work had to stop. Setting aside normal jobs gave the entire community time to gather and focus on the Lord. Pausing our daily labor honors God as the true source of our provision.

On each of the feast days, Israel brought a burnt offering of two young bulls, one ram, and seven male lambs, all completely free of flaws. Each animal was offered with its proper measure of fine flour mixed with oil. These large offerings showed deep gratitude for God's great redemption.

A male goat was also sacrificed each day as a sin offering to make atonement for the people. Atonement means restoring a broken relationship with God by covering and wiping away sin. It taught Israel that even during sacred festivals, holy people still depend on God's cleansing grace.

These special feast sacrifices were offered every morning for seven days, always in addition to the daily morning and evening lambs. On the seventh day, the feast ended with another sacred assembly and rest from regular work. Dedicating the entire week to God showed that celebration and worship belong together.

On the day of firstfruits, also known as the Feast of Weeks or Pentecost, the people held a sacred assembly and rested from daily work. Coming seven weeks after Passover, this festival celebrated the early wheat harvest by presenting loaves made of new grain to the Lord. It taught Israel to thank God first before enjoying the harvest for themselves.

The burnt offerings for this harvest feast matched those of the new moon and Unleavened Bread: two young bulls, one ram, and seven yearling lambs. Each animal was offered with its proper grain portion of fine flour mixed with oil. Presenting such generous gifts showed heartfelt thanks for God's abundant provision in the fields.

A male goat was sacrificed alongside the harvest offerings to make atonement for the nation. Even while rejoicing over a full harvest, the worshipers remembered their need to be right with God. True spiritual joy always goes hand in hand with humble confession of sin.

All of these festival sacrifices were offered in addition to the daily morning and evening offerings. Every animal, as well as the flour, oil, and wine, had to be completely unblemished and pure. God deserves our very best devotion, offered with sincere hearts and reverent care.
